key.title: Key
key.plain: The home note a piece keeps returning to, together with the set of notes that sound at home with it. A tune in a key feels finished when it lands on that home note.

scale.title: Scale
scale.plain: The notes of a key in order, from the home note up to the same note higher. Each scale has its own pattern of big and small steps, which gives it its colour.

root.title: Root
root.plain: The note a scale or a chord is built on, and named after. Everything else is counted up from it.

keySignature.title: Key signature
keySignature.plain: The sharps or flats written once at the start of each line of music; they apply to every note with that letter. Any other sharp or flat is written beside its note, and some scales have no key signature of their own.

sharpFlat.title: Sharp ♯ and flat ♭
sharpFlat.plain: A sharp raises a note to the very next key up on a piano (a half step); a flat lowers it to the next key down. They are written before the note, or once in the key signature.

halfStep.title: Half step and whole step
halfStep.plain: A half step is the smallest step: from one piano key to the very next one, black or white. A whole step is two half steps. Scales are built from these steps.
halfStep.example: In {{key}}, {{a}} to {{b}} is a half step.
halfStep.exampleWhole: In {{key}}, {{a}} to {{b}} is a whole step.

octave.title: Octave
octave.plain: The same note name, higher or lower: the two sound so alike that they share a name. The last column of the scale is the home note again, an octave up.
octave.example: {{root}} and the next {{root}} up are an octave apart.

staff.title: Staff
staff.plain: The five lines music is written on. The higher a note sits on the lines, the higher it sounds; the sign at the start (the clef) fixes which note each line is.

interval.title: Interval
interval.plain: The distance between two notes, counted by letter names with both ends included: three letters apart is a 3rd. In labels, m means minor (smaller), M major (larger), P perfect.

tritone.title: Tritone
tritone.plain: Two notes three whole steps (six half steps) apart: a tense sound that wants to move on. In the notes of the scale it marks a 5th note that is a half step lower than usual.

relativeKey.title: Relative key
relativeKey.plain: A major key and a minor key that use exactly the same notes, from a different home note. The minor one starts three half steps below the major one.
relativeKey.only: Only major and minor keys have a relative key.

dominantKey.title: Dominant key
dominantKey.plain: The key that starts on the 5th note of this one. It differs from this key by just one note, so music often travels there and comes back.
dominantKey.only: Major and minor keys have a dominant key; this scale does not.

subdominantKey.title: Subdominant key
subdominantKey.plain: The key that starts on the 4th note of this one. Like the dominant key, it differs from this key by just one note.
subdominantKey.only: Major and minor keys have a subdominant key; this scale does not.

parentKey.title: Parent key
parentKey.plain: The major key whose notes a mode uses. The notes are the same; the mode simply treats a different one as home, which changes the mood.
parentKey.only: Only the modes (Dorian, Phrygian, Lydian, Mixolydian, Locrian) have a parent key here.

circleOfFifths.title: Circle of fifths
circleOfFifths.plain: The twelve keys in a ring, so that neighbours share all their notes but one. Going round clockwise, each key starts a 5th (seven half steps) higher, and the key signature changes by one sharp or flat.

relatedKeys.title: Shared notes
relatedKeys.plain: How many notes two keys have in common. Neighbours on the circle share six of seven, so moving between them sounds smooth; keys far apart share few and sound distant.

mode.title: Mode
mode.plain: A scale made by taking the notes of another scale (most often the major scale) and treating a different one of them as home. Same notes, a different mood.

classicalMinor.title: Ascending and descending
classicalMinor.plain: Classical melodic minor raises its 6th and 7th notes on the way up, for a smooth climb to home, and lowers them again on the way down. Jazz keeps them raised both ways.

writtenOctave.title: Written an octave higher
writtenOctave.plain: Guitar music is written one octave above the notes that actually sound, so that it fits on the treble staff. The small 8 under the clef says so.

degree.title: Scale degree (1–7)
degree.plain: A note's number in the scale, counting up from the home note, which is 1. A ♭ or ♯ beside the number (♭3) means a half step lower or higher than in the major scale.

tonic.title: Tonic
tonic.plain: The home note, number 1. A tune sounds finished when it lands there, and the key is named after it.

supertonic.title: Supertonic
supertonic.plain: The 2nd note, one step above home. It often leads back down to home, or on towards the dominant.

mediant.title: Mediant
mediant.plain: The 3rd note, halfway from home to the dominant. Whether it is three or four half steps above home largely decides whether the scale sounds dark or bright.

subdominant.title: Subdominant
subdominant.plain: The 4th note. The chord built on it moves away from home, often on the way to the dominant chord.

dominant.title: Dominant
dominant.plain: The 5th note, and the chord built on it. After home it is the most important note: its chord sounds open, like a question that the home chord answers.

submediant.title: Submediant
submediant.plain: The 6th note. Its chord shares two notes with the home chord, so it can stand in for home with a softer colour.

leadingNote.title: Leading note
leadingNote.plain: The 7th note when it sits just a half step below home. It pulls up into home so strongly that a tune stopping on it sounds unfinished.

subtonic.title: Subtonic
subtonic.plain: The 7th note when it is a whole step below home. Without the half-step pull of a leading note it sounds relaxed rather than urgent.

augFifth.title: Augmented 5th
augFifth.plain: A 5th note that is a half step higher than usual (eight half steps above home). It sounds unsettled and wants to move.

chord.title: Chord
chord.plain: Three or more notes sounding together. Most chords are built by stacking every other note of a scale: a note, the one two letters up, and the one two letters above that.

chordsInKey.title: Chords in the key
chordsInKey.plain: The chords you can build from the key's own notes: start on each note of the scale and stack every other note above it. Songs in a key mostly use these chords.

romanNumeral.title: Roman numerals (I, ii, V…)
romanNumeral.plain: They number a chord by the scale note it starts on: I on the 1st note, V on the 5th. Capitals mean a major chord, small letters a minor one, ° a diminished one.

triad.title: Triad
triad.plain: A chord of three notes: the root, the note a 3rd above it and the note a 5th above it. Most chords in pop and folk songs are triads.

majorChord.title: Major chord
majorChord.plain: Three notes played together, with a bright, settled sound. The middle note is four frets (or four piano keys, counting black and white) above the note that names the chord.

minorChord.title: Minor chord
minorChord.plain: Three notes played together, with a darker or sadder sound. The middle note is three frets (or three piano keys, counting black and white) above the note that names the chord: one fewer than in a major chord.

diminishedChord.title: Diminished chord
diminishedChord.plain: A chord built from small 3rds (three half steps each) stacked up. It sounds tense and unstable, as if it must move on.

augmentedChord.title: Augmented chord
augmentedChord.plain: A chord built from large 3rds (four half steps each) stacked up. It sounds dreamy and unresolved.

seventhChord.title: Seventh chord
seventhChord.plain: A triad with one more note on top, a 7th above the root. The extra note adds colour or tension; which 7th, over which triad, gives each kind its name.

dominantSeventh.title: Dominant 7th (7)
dominantSeventh.plain: A major chord plus the note ten half steps above the root. It is the chord on the 5th note of a major key, and it pulls hard towards home.

majorSeventh.title: Major 7th (maj7)
majorSeventh.plain: A major chord plus the note eleven half steps above the root (a half step below the next root up). Soft and dreamy, common in jazz and soul.

minorSeventh.title: Minor 7th (m7)
minorSeventh.plain: A minor chord plus the note ten half steps above the root. Mellow and smooth.

halfDiminished.title: Half-diminished (m7♭5)
halfDiminished.plain: A diminished triad plus the note ten half steps above the root. In a major key it is the chord on the 7th note.

diminishedSeventh.title: Diminished 7th (dim7)
diminishedSeventh.plain: Four notes, each three half steps above the last, so they split the octave evenly. Very tense; it can lead to many different chords.

sixthChord.title: Sixth chord (6, m6, 6/9)
sixthChord.plain: A major or minor chord plus the note nine half steps above the root (the 6th); 6/9 adds the 9th as well. Sweet and rounded, a favourite ending in swing.

susChord.title: Suspended chord (sus)
susChord.plain: A chord whose middle note is replaced by the 2nd or the 4th. Neither major nor minor, it sounds open, as if waiting to settle.

powerChord.title: Power chord (5)
powerChord.plain: Just the root and the 5th, often with the root again on top. With no 3rd it is neither major nor minor: the basic chord of rock guitar.

addedNote.title: Added note (add9, add11)
addedNote.plain: A plain chord with one extra note added (the 9th is the 2nd an octave up, the 11th the 4th), without the 7th that bigger chords would include.

extendedChord.title: Extended chord (9, 11, 13)
extendedChord.plain: A seventh chord with more notes stacked on top: the 9th, 11th and 13th are the 2nd, 4th and 6th an octave higher. Rich and jazzy.

alteredChord.title: Altered chord (♭5, ♯5, ♭9, ♯9, alt)
alteredChord.plain: A chord with some notes moved a half step from their usual place, shown by ♭ or ♯ in its name (or 'alt'). The moved notes add tension, usually just before the chord it leads to.

inversion.title: Inversion
inversion.plain: The same chord with a different note at the bottom. Root position has the root lowest; the 1st inversion puts the 3rd lowest, the 2nd the 5th. Same chord, a slightly different colour.

formula.title: Formula (R 3 5)
formula.plain: What a chord is made of, counted from its root: R is the root, 3 the note a 3rd above, 5 a 5th above. ♭3 or ♭7 mean a half step lower than in the major scale.

arpeggio.title: Arpeggio
arpeggio.plain: A chord played one note at a time, from the bottom up, instead of all together.

compatibleScales.title: Compatible scales
compatibleScales.plain: Scales whose notes fit over this chord, for a tune or a solo above it. Choosing one makes it the scale on screen, starting from the chord's root.

slashChord.title: Slash chord
slashChord.plain: A chord with a chosen note at the bottom, written after a slash: the name before the slash is the chord, the note after it is the lowest one played.

outOfKey.title: Out of key
outOfKey.plain: A chord that uses at least one note from outside the key's scale. It brings a surprising colour; songs use such chords on purpose.

fret.title: Fret
fret.plain: The metal strips across a guitar's neck. Pressing a string just behind fret 3 plays the note three half steps above the open string, which is played without pressing (0).

position.title: Position (I, II, V…)
position.plain: Where your hand sits on the neck, named by a Roman numeral for the fret your 1st finger covers: in position V it is fret 5. Open position uses the open strings and the first frets.

fingerNumbers.title: Finger numbers
fingerNumbers.plain: The numbers on the dots say which finger of the fretting hand plays each note: 1 index, 2 middle, 3 ring, 4 little finger; 0 is an open string.

stretch.title: Stretch
stretch.plain: A note one fret beyond the hand's usual four-fret span: the hand reaches out for it without moving.

tuning.title: Tuning
tuning.plain: The notes the six open strings are set to. Standard tuning is E A D G B E from the thickest string; other tunings change some strings for a different sound.

anchorFret.title: Starting fret (3fr)
anchorFret.plain: The number beside a chord shape, such as 3fr, says which fret the shape starts at, so you know where on the neck to play it.

tirandoApoyando.title: Tirando and apoyando
tirandoApoyando.plain: Two ways to pluck with the right hand: tirando (free stroke) lifts the finger clear of the strings; apoyando (rest stroke) lets it come to rest on the next string, for a fuller tone.

rightHandFingers.title: p, i, m, a
rightHandFingers.plain: The right-hand fingers, by the first letters of their Spanish names (pulgar, índice, medio, anular): p thumb, i index, m middle, a ring. Alternating i–m means plucking with index and middle in turn.

positionWalk.title: Position walk
positionWalk.plain: A scale played through several hand positions one after another, sliding one finger along a string to move from each position to the next.

technicalSet.title: Technical set
technicalSet.plain: Scales, arpeggios and broken chords to practise in one key, like the technical work of a mid-level guitar exam (grade 5 of the UK exam boards).

intervalScale.title: Scale in 3rds, 6ths, octaves
intervalScale.plain: The scale played in pairs of notes a 3rd, a 6th or an octave apart: one after the other (broken) or both at once (together).

brokenChord.title: Broken chord
brokenChord.plain: A chord's notes played one or a few at a time in a pattern, instead of all together.

progression.title: Progression
progression.plain: Chords played one after another, in the order a song uses them. Its numbers in the key (such as I–V–vi–IV) stay the same when it moves to another key.

tempo.title: Tempo
tempo.plain: How fast the music goes, counted in beats a minute: 60 is one beat a second, 120 is two beats a second.

capo.title: Capo
capo.plain: A clamp across all the strings at one fret. The open strings then sound higher, so the same chord shapes sound in a higher key: G shapes with a capo on fret 2 sound in A.

transpose.title: Moving to another key (transposing)
transpose.plain: Playing the same chords or tune higher or lower: every note moves by the same number of half steps, so the numbers (I, IV, V) stay the same.

scale_major.plain: The bright, everyday scale of most songs: whole steps everywhere except two half steps, between notes 3–4 and 7–8.

scale_natural_minor.plain: The darker partner of major: its 3rd, 6th and 7th notes are a half step lower. It has the same notes as the major scale that starts on its 3rd note.

scale_harmonic_minor.plain: Natural minor with its 7th note raised a half step, so it leans into home as major does. The wide gap between its 6th and 7th notes gives it a dramatic colour.

scale_melodic_minor.plain: Natural minor with its 6th and 7th notes raised, for a smooth climb to home. Classical music lowers them again on the way down; jazz keeps them raised.

scale_dorian.plain: A minor scale with a brighter 6th note than natural minor. A mellow minor, heard in folk, funk and jazz.

scale_phrygian.plain: A minor scale whose 2nd note is only a half step above home, which gives it a dark, tense colour, common in flamenco and metal.

scale_lydian.plain: A major scale with its 4th note raised a half step: bright and floating, a favourite of film music.

scale_mixolydian.plain: A major scale with its 7th note lowered a half step, so it has no strong pull back home: relaxed and bluesy, common in rock and folk.

scale_locrian.plain: The darkest mode: its 2nd note is a half step above home and its 5th is lowered, so even its home chord sounds unstable. Rarely used for whole pieces.

scale_pentatonic_major.plain: Five notes: the major scale without its 4th and 7th. With no half steps, almost any order of its notes sounds good; folk songs all over the world use it.

scale_pentatonic_minor.plain: Five notes: natural minor without its 2nd and 6th. The basic scale of rock and blues solos.

scale_blues.plain: Minor pentatonic plus one extra note between its 4th and 5th (the 'blue note'), which gives the blues its gritty sound.

scale_major_blues.plain: Major pentatonic plus one extra note between its 2nd and 3rd, for a bright scale with a bluesy flavour.

scale_whole_tone.plain: Six notes, each a whole step from the next. With no half steps to pull towards home it sounds dreamy and floating.

scale_diminished_whole_half.plain: Eight notes, alternating a whole step and a half step. Even and tense; jazz uses it over diminished chords.

scale_diminished_half_whole.plain: Eight notes, alternating a half step and a whole step. Jazz uses it over dominant 7th chords for a tense, crunchy sound.

scale_chromatic.plain: All twelve notes in order, each a half step from the next: every key of the piano, black and white, in one octave.

scale_altered.plain: A jazz scale (the 7th mode of melodic minor) that changes every note of a dominant 7th chord that can be changed, for the most tension just before home.

scale_lydian_dominant.plain: Lydian with a lowered 7th, or Mixolydian with a raised 4th: bright and bluesy at once. The 4th mode of melodic minor.

scale_phrygian_dominant.plain: Phrygian with a raised 3rd, so its home chord is major: a sound heard in flamenco and in much Middle Eastern music. The 5th mode of harmonic minor.

scale_locrian_natural2.plain: Locrian with its 2nd note a whole step above home: a dark minor scale used in jazz over half-diminished chords. The 6th mode of melodic minor.

scale_bebop_dominant.plain: Mixolydian with one extra note between its 7th and home, so a run of quick even notes lands chord notes on the beats.

scale_bebop_major.plain: The major scale with one extra note between its 5th and 6th, so a run of quick even notes lands chord notes on the beats.

scale_bebop_dorian.plain: Dorian with one extra note between its 3rd and 4th, so a run of quick even notes lands chord notes on the beats.

scale_dorian_b2.plain: Dorian with its 2nd note only a half step above home: dark and exotic. The 2nd mode of melodic minor.

scale_lydian_augmented.plain: Lydian with its 5th raised as well: very bright and unsettled. The 3rd mode of melodic minor.

scale_mixolydian_b6.plain: Mixolydian with a lowered 6th: major in its lower half, minor in its upper half. The 5th mode of melodic minor.

scale_hungarian_minor.plain: Harmonic minor with a raised 4th. Its two wide gaps give it a dramatic colour heard in Central European folk music.

scale_hungarian_major.plain: A major-sounding scale with a raised 2nd, a raised 4th and a lowered 7th: bright but strange, with a wide gap right after home.

scale_double_harmonic.plain: A wide gap after the 2nd note and another after the 6th, each with a half step on both sides: the sound often called Arabic or Byzantine.

scale_persian.plain: Like the double harmonic scale with a lowered 5th: half steps and wide gaps side by side, for a dark, intense colour.

scale_neapolitan_minor.plain: Harmonic minor with its 2nd note lowered to a half step above home: dark and dramatic.

scale_neapolitan_major.plain: Melodic minor with its 2nd note lowered to a half step above home: dark at the bottom, bright at the top.

scale_hirajoshi.plain: A five-note scale from Japan, with two half steps and two wide gaps. It is often used for a calm, haunting sound.

scale_in_sen.plain: A five-note scale from Japan that starts with a half step: quiet and mysterious.

scale_iwato.plain: A five-note scale from Japan with two half steps and a lowered 5th: the darkest of the Japanese scales here.

scale_egyptian.plain: A five-note scale with no 3rd and no 6th, so it is neither major nor minor: open and ancient-sounding.
